narrative: Monday, 2:14 PM. The service map was complete and in the engagement log — eight entries, eight confirmed software identities, all documented with both banner and -sV results.
James leaned back from his keyboard. 'We found everything,' he said. 'Two hosts. All open ports. All the service versions. Maya — we know what's running on every port.'
Maya looked up from her notes.
'No,' she said. 'We found the doors. Now we need to discover which ones are actually weak.'
James frowned. 'But we have the version numbers. Can't we just search them up and see what's vulnerable?'

'We can search them up,' Maya said. 'But searching for a version number is the beginning of a research process — not the end of one. Before you open a CVE database, I want you to think about what you are actually asking.'
She turned to face him fully.
'What does it mean for a server to be vulnerable?'
James thought about it. 'There is... a security issue in the software it is running?'

'That is a weakness,' Maya said. 'A vulnerability is more specific. It means the weakness is present in this installation, in this configuration, reachable from this position, with no other control blocking it. A weakness that exists in the software but cannot be reached from where we are is not something we can exploit. A weakness that requires a feature the server has disabled is not something we can trigger. A weakness that has been patched — even if the version number looks old — may not be exploitable at all.'
James was quiet for a moment. 'So finding a CVE for Apache 2.4.49 does not automatically mean this server is vulnerable to it.'
'Exactly,' Maya said. 'It means there is a potential match that requires confirmation. That confirmation process — systematic, evidence-based, documented — is vulnerability assessment.'
She opened her browser. nvd.nist.gov.
'Before we search,' she said, 'tell me what you expect to find when we search for Apache httpd 2.4.49. Be specific.'
James thought about it. 'I think... a lot of results? Apache has been around forever. There must be hundreds of vulnerabilities. We are probably vulnerable to something.'
Maya typed: apache httpd 2.4.49
The results loaded. Not hundreds — a targeted list, because 2.4.49 is a specific version, not a software family. CVE results for this exact release. The first entry caught them both.
CVE-2021-41773. Apache HTTP Server 2.4.49. Path traversal and remote code execution. CVSS: 9.8.
James stared at it. '9.8. That is...'

'Critical,' Maya said. 'The highest range. But before we document anything — three questions.' She turned to him. 'Three questions that every professional asks before a CVE becomes a finding. By the end of this mission, you will know what they are — and why they matter more than the score.'

characters.name: Maya Patel
characters.description: Six years of experience. Maya had seen teams celebrate CVE findings before confirming them — and watched those celebrations turn into client complaints when the report was challenged.

characters.name: James Okafor
characters.description: Fourth week of his first real engagement. James has the version numbers. He is learning what to do with them.
